messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] HDP in stan ("no acceptable small step size...")
parts:
Thanks for trying Stan.  

When I see the stick process definition, I am afraid you would have discrete parameters, which is not supported in Stan for now.  But I did not.

However, in the following model block, z is neither data nor parameter, but contributes to the log-posterior, which I think is problematic. 

--
Jiqiqang


model {
    # stick lengths for stick-breaking prior
    for (k in 1:K) {
        b1[k] ~ beta(1, gamma[k]);
    }

    # per-topic word distributions
    for (k in 1:K) {
        theta[k] ~ dirichlet(H);
    }

    for (d in 1:D) {
        # per-document topic weights
        pi[d] ~ dirichlet(alpha .* beta);

        for (n in 1:N[d]) {
            int z;
            z ~ categorical(pi[d]);
            w[d,n] ~ categorical(theta[z]);
        }
    }
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] HDP in stan ("no acceptable small step size...")
parts:
Yes, that's definitely the problem. Unfortunately, Stan at present
doesn't support discrete latent variables, and so can't handle
hierarchical mixture models. Gibbs sampling for discrete latent
variables is planned for a future release, but even then it may be
fairly inefficient, since we don't at present compute the Markov
blanket for each latent variable.

Best,
Matt

messages.subject: discrete parameters hack
parts:
On Friday, September 28, 2012 11:00:36 AM UTC-4, Matt Hoffman wrote:
Yes, that's definitely the problem. Unfortunately, Stan at present
doesn't support discrete latent variables, and so can't handle
hierarchical mixture models. Gibbs sampling for discrete latent
variables is planned for a future release, but even then it may be
fairly inefficient, since we don't at present compute the Markov
blanket for each latent variable.

Matt3 (or anyone else),

How badly would you expect the following hack for sampling integer parameters to work?

data {
  // something
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0.5, upper = 10.5> theta;
}
transformed parameters {
  int<lower=1,upper=10> theta_int;
  theta_int <- round(theta);
}
model {
  // pseudo-prior on theta
  lp__ <- lp__ + log1p(cos(2 * pi() * theta));

  // log-likelihood of data as a function of theta_int
}

We talked on stan-dev about the difficulties of multimodal posteriors, but presume the log-likelihood is unimodalish in theta_int here. Since the pseudo-prior on theta discourages the points of discontinuity in the round() function, do you think Stan could leapfrog effectively across the nearly integer values in theta-space?

Ben

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] discrete parameters hack
parts:
It could work in theory (i.e., as the chain length goes to infinity it should converge because detailed balance and ergodicity should still hold for the HMC transition kernel), but the sampler is likely to perform very poorly for finite chains.  Rejection rates will be high near the rounding boundaries making it hard to transition between discrete parameter values resulting in poor mixing which may be very hard to diagnose.  It's also likely that the stepsize adaptation of NUTS2 may behave badly near rounding boundaries.

Personally, I wouldn't recommend people use it for real work due to the likelihood of incorrect results that may be hard to notice.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] discrete parameters hack
parts:
>>> How badly would you expect the following hack for sampling integer parameters to work?
>>>
>>>

>>> parameters {
>>> real<lower=0.5, upper = 10.5> theta;
>>> }
>>> transformed parameters {
>>> int<lower=1,upper=10> theta_int;
>>> theta_int <- round(theta);
>>> }
>>> model {
>>> // pseudo-prior on theta
>>> lp__ <- lp__ + log1p(cos(2 * pi() * theta));
>>>
>>> // log-likelihood of data as a function of theta_int
>>> }

As Jonatahan Esterhazy pointed out, this won't work in Stan because
we don't allow int params or transformed params.

I believe the intent is the same as that of the following model,
which is legal:

parameters {
real<lower=0.5, upper = 10.5> theta;
}

model {
int theta_int_local;
theta_int_local <- round(theta);

// pseudo-prior on theta
lp__ <- lp__ + log1p(cos(2 * pi() * theta));

// log-likelihood of data as a function of theta_int_local
}
generated quantities {

int<lower=1,upper=10> theta_int;
theta_int <- round(theta);
}

There are a couple of problems, though, with modeling.

First, the

int round(real);

function loses the gradient. So any information in the log
likelihood won't be transmitted back through to sampling.
This is really the dealbreaker.

Now if you can express the model in terms of the continuous
value, for instance as in the Albert and Chib latent
parameter approach to ordinal probit, then this kind of
thing will work.

I wonder how many other cases we could handle with some
kind of latent value? I'd think it'd only make sense for
ordinal (or binary) responses.

- Bob
